question: What local natural-diet evidence does the Lake Mainit snakehead study provide, and can its fish category establish cannibalism or be published as Bangwit diet content?

source.citation: Paglinawan, R. J., Paylangco, R. A., Paylangco, J. C., Along, A. A., & Almadin, F. J. (2022). Association of size structure, diet composition, endo-parasites of Snakehead fish (Channa striata, Bloch), in Lake Mainit, Caraga Region, Philippines. Southeastern Philippines Journal of Research and Development, 27(2), 1-22. https://doi.org/10.53899/spjrd.v27i2.135
source.fullTextProvenance: The official publisher-hosted PDF was available and reviewed. No third-party mirror, article image or PDF copy is stored in the repository.

licenseReview.policyTextSummary: The journal policy page states CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and describes redistribution of the article in unadapted form for noncommercial use with attribution. The same policy page's copyright section also says authors may remix, transform and build upon material for any purpose; this creates an unresolved policy/rights ambiguity.
licenseReview.decision: Do not adapt or reproduce the article's tables, figures or text in the app. Item-specific scope and the policy inconsistency need qualified review before any reuse; no permission is inferred.

source.studyArea: Lake Mainit, Caraga Region; sampled municipalities were Jabonga and Kitcharao in Agusan del Norte and Mainit in Surigao del Norte.

sampling.gearAndSelection: Wild fish were purposively collected with local fishers using gillnets; the paper reports at least 30 fish per municipality per index season over a one-week town-level collection interval.
sampling.dietMethod: Stomach contents were removed, counted, and grouped under microscopy into seven broad categories. The analysis reports occurrence, number, volume and an Index of Relative Importance (IRI).
sampling.localityNaming: Methods name Barangay Poblacion (Jabonga), Barangay Jaliobong (Kitcharao), and Barangay Mansa-yao (Mainit); figure captions also spell the latter two names Jaliobong/Jalibobong and Mansa-yao/Mainsayao/Mansayao. No coordinates or sample-to-barangay diet crosswalk were extracted.

observations.evidenceType: Stomach-content examination of sampled wild fish; not direct observation of feeding and not a bait trial.
observations.reportedPattern: The authors identify shrimp as the leading IRI food category in both seasonal groups. The article reports fish, plant material, crab and detritus in the sampled contents; aquatic insects and snails are reported only in the wet-season group.
observations.preyIdentity: The study does not identify fish remains to species. It therefore supports fish consumption in these Lake Mainit samples, but does not establish that Channa striata ate its own species.
observations.numericTableCheck: Table 1 lists wet-season shrimp IRI as 47.16, while nearby results prose gives 47.52. The displayed IRI entries sum to 80.19 for the dry group and 119.80 for the wet group, rather than 100 in either group. The rank statement is retained as the paper's reported conclusion; the percentage values are held pending clarification and are not imported as app-ready data.
observations.siteAndSeasonResolution: The study includes three municipalities and two sampling rounds, but the diet table is pooled across selected municipalities; it does not provide a per-municipality food profile. The article labels groups dry/wet while naming June and November collection dates; no unambiguous month-to-season mapping is asserted here.

decision.reason: This is useful, direct historical gut-content evidence for Lake Mainit Channa striata, but its fish prey remains unidentified, the diet table has numerical inconsistencies, the food profile is not municipality-specific, and the journal's posted reuse policy is restrictive and internally ambiguous. No app display or derivative reuse is approved.

limitations: The observations describe 180 fish sampled in 2019 and are not current monitoring or a species-wide diet guarantee.
Fish was a broad gut-content category; no prey species or conspecific Channa prey was identified.
Diet results are pooled across the selected Lake Mainit municipalities; no per-site diet crosswalk or exact sample coordinates were extracted.
The reported IRI value for wet-season shrimp differs between prose and Table 1, and the displayed season totals are not normalized to 100.
The paper varies in spelling the barangay names in its methods and figure captions.
The posted journal licensing and copyright language is not fully consistent, and the PDF does not show a separately captured article-level license notice.
No bait advice, legal catchability, water quality, current safety, occurrence geometry or current abundance can be inferred from this diet study.
nextAction: Keep the Lake Mainit diet evidence research-only. Continue Caraga inland research with another primary freshwater source, and keep any cross-study synthesis separate from app admission until rights and product review are resolved.

references.supports: Publisher-hosted full article: study citation, sampling locations and methods, stomach-content categories, reported seasonal pattern, Table 1 and internal numerical discrepancy.
Publisher article record, DOI, publication date, authors, issue and abstract.
Journal-wide open-access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licensing and copyright policy language; not a separately captured article-level rights determination.
